questions.question:
#include <stdio.h>
void foo(int *p, int x) {
    *p = x;
}

int main() {
    int *z;
    int a = 20, b = 25;
    z = &a;
    foo(z, b);
    printf("%d", a);
    return 0;
}
The output of the given C program is __________. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
[latex]\text{z}=\&\text{a}[/latex] makes [latex]z[/latex] point to [latex]a[/latex] (currently [latex]20[/latex]).

[latex]\text{foo(z, b)}[/latex] passes [latex]z[/latex] (the address of [latex]a[/latex]) and [latex]b[/latex]'s value ([latex]25[/latex]) into [latex]\text{foo(int *p, int x)}[/latex], so inside [latex]\text{foo}[/latex], [latex]p[/latex] points to [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]x=25[/latex].

[latex]{*}\text{p}=\text{x}[/latex] writes [latex]25[/latex] into whatever [latex]p[/latex] points to — i.e. directly into [latex]a[/latex] itself (since pointers give real access to the caller's variable). So [latex]a[/latex] becomes [latex]25[/latex].

[latex]\text{printf}[/latex] then prints the now-updated [latex]a[/latex].

Answer: 25

Consider the following statements:

I. The smallest element in a max-heap is always at a leaf node.
II. The second largest element in a max-heap is always a child of the root node.
III. A max-heap can be constructed from a binary search tree in [latex]\Theta (n)[/latex] time.

Checking each statement:
- I: a node with a child is larger than that child, so the minimum has no child [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] it is a leaf [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- II: the 2nd largest can only be smaller than the root, so its parent must be the root [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- III: build-heap on any array (e.g. the BST's elements) takes [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- IV: a BST from a heap in [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] would give an [latex]O(n)[/latex] comparison sort (inorder traversal) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: I, II and III

questions.question:
Let [latex]P[/latex] be the set of all integers from [latex]1[/latex] to [latex]15[/latex]. Consider any order of insertion of the elements of [latex]P[/latex] into a binary search tree that creates a complete binary tree.

Which one of the following elements can NEVER be the third element that is inserted?
questions.explanation:
Since the [latex]15[/latex] elements form a complete binary tree that is also a valid BST, the shape and contents of every position are fully determined: the tree must be a perfectly balanced BST on [latex]\{1,\ldots,15\}[/latex]:

Level 0 (root): [latex]8[/latex]
Level 1: [latex]4,\ 12[/latex]
Level 2: [latex]2,\ 6,\ 10,\ 14[/latex]
Level 3 (leaves): [latex]1,3,5,7,9,11,13,15[/latex]

For an insertion sequence to build up exactly this shape via ordinary BST insertion, a node can only be inserted after its parent has already been inserted (a node's tree position is only "unlocked" once its parent exists). So valid insertion orders are precisely the orders in which every node appears after its parent (a topological/level-respecting order).

The root [latex]8[/latex] must always be inserted first. The second insertion must be one of the root's children, [latex]4[/latex] or [latex]12[/latex]. The third insertion can then be: the other level-1 node ([latex]12[/latex] or [latex]4[/latex]), or a level-2 child of whichever level-1 node was inserted second (e.g. [latex]2[/latex] or [latex]6[/latex] if [latex]4[/latex] went second). This gives possible third elements [latex]\{2,4,6,10,12,14\}[/latex] — only levels 0-2 nodes can ever appear as early as the third insertion.

[latex]5[/latex] is a level-3 leaf (child of [latex]6[/latex], which is itself a level-2 child of [latex]4[/latex]). Before [latex]5[/latex] can be inserted, both its ancestors [latex]8[/latex] and [latex]4[/latex] and [latex]6[/latex] would already need to exist — requiring at least [latex]4[/latex] prior insertions. So [latex]5[/latex] can never be inserted as early as third.

Answer: 5 can NEVER be the third element inserted.
